stepsize_control_alpha2._purpose: Controls the step-size confound: at K=2 with alpha=1/255 the counterattack can only travel 2/255 inside a 4/255 budget, i.e. the baseline never reaches the constraint boundary. This block doubles alpha.
stepsize_control_alpha2._reading: Doubling alpha alone lifts TTC from 6.88 to 22.65, i.e. ABOVE NAC's default-configuration 17.15. Matching alpha between the two methods still leaves NAC ahead (33.98 vs 22.65, +11.33pp), so the solver effect survives -- but the paper's headline '+9.75pp at K=2' is largely reproducible by tuning the baseline's step size, and MUST be reported alongside this control.

K4_control._note: At K=4 a generic adaptive optimizer reaches 37.50 +/- 0.55 vs NAC's 37.70 (seed 0) -- statistically indistinguishable. NAC's optimizer claim is therefore confined to the small-K regime; it must not be stated as 'NAC is the best optimizer tested'.
K4_control._update_2026_10_13: NAC now has 3 seeds at K=4 alpha=1/255 (see k4_optimizer_grid_3seed): 37.50+/-0.24. Conclusion unchanged: only bias-uncorrected RMSProp ties NAC at K=4; Adam/AdaGrad stay ~14pp below.

optimizer_comparison.key_finding: CORRECTED 2026-10. Two claims are supported and one is not. SUPPORTED: (1) at matched alpha and K, NAC beats TTC (alpha=1/255: 17.15 vs 6.88; alpha=2/255: 33.98 vs 22.65); (2) Adam and AdaGrad both fall BELOW the TTC baseline (5.53 and 6.60 vs 6.88), so generic adaptive optimization is not automatically beneficial here. NOT SUPPORTED: the claim that momentum acceleration rather than generic optimizer improvement drives the gain -- RMSProp reaches 31.45 at identical K/alpha/eps/bs/seeds, and the bias-corrected control (8.65) shows that deficit is a step-length artefact that applies equally to NAC's own velocity accumulation, which was never given the same correction. At K=4 RMSProp (37.50) is indistinguishable from NAC (37.70).

adaptive_attack_pilot.description: Defense-aware adaptive PGD pilot (first-order, CLIP-MAD-motivated): at each attack step the adversary re-runs the defense's counterattack (stop-gradient; the counterattack acts as a fixed operator) and optimizes cross-entropy against the DEFENDED prediction, then updates the perturbation. Closes the 'no adaptive attack' gap (the only remaining item from the 2026-10 GPT review checklist).

adaptive_attack_pilot.key_finding: Under a first-order defense-aware attack all test-time defenses shrink drastically (industry-wide, consistent with CLIP-MAD's overestimation claim), but the relative ordering is preserved: NAC/TTC ~ 2.7x, so NAC's comparative advantage is not a gradient-masking artefact.
adaptive_attack_pilot._limitations: First-order (no expectation over defense random init), single seed, CIFAR-10 only; not a full reproduction of CLIP-MAD's second-order attack. Disclosed as such in the paper Limitations.
adaptive_attack_pilot._references: arxiv sec:adaptive (L362-377, tab:adaptive) + Limitations 'Adaptive attack scope'; 8page L275; single_preview L275; chinese L294.

mechanism_diagnostic.description: Per-step gradient mechanistic diagnostic. Key honest findings: NAC's successive-gradient autocorrelation (0.169) far exceeds TTC's essentially-random level (0.027, ~= random-anchor control -0.048); NAC step-to-landing-gradient alignment exceeds TTC's (+0.059). BUT the look-ahead gradient's predictiveness for the next iterate is NOT better than the current position (predictiveness gain -0.051, i.e. chance level), so the benefit is attributed to trajectory coherence / farther aligned displacement, NOT to the look-ahead being a sharper estimate. Reported as diagnostics, not proven causal mechanism.
mechanism_diagnostic.references: arxiv sec:mechanism (new), Why NAC Works (harmonized); 8page L263; single_preview L264; chinese sec:optfamily_cn.
mechanism_diagnostic._note: Corrects earlier varguer 'walks further not more accurate' phrasing with the precise measurement: coherent direction + farther displacement, look-ahead not sharper. Replaced the older paper claim that the look-ahead gradient is a 'more reliable estimate of the next gradient'.

_honest_notes: MAC official code does not support CIFAR-10; this row comes from the ported implementation whose DTD reproduction is bit-exact.
Defense budget is DOUBLE ours (eps=8/255 vs 4/255) and 2 views double the forward cost; not a like-for-like comparison with TTC/NAC/DOC rows.
Attack uses 100 steps (MAC published protocol) vs the 10-step protocol of all other rows; undefended accuracy is 0.00 under both (attack saturated).

Port fidelity is verified only at the published config (DTD bit-exact); disclose this row as a diagnostic.

budget_matched_dual_caliber.description: Same-budget cross-method comparison, CIFAR-10, PGD-10 eps=4/255, bs=32. Answers 'is NAC behind DOC/MAC?': under matched budgets NAC leads at both tested budget points.
budget_matched_dual_caliber.key_finding: Published-config ordering (MAC 44.89 > DOC 37.45 > NAC 16.77) reverses under matched budgets: at DOC's budget NAC 40.01 > DOC 37.45 > TTC 34.59; at NAC's budget NAC 17.17 > TTC 7.05 > MAC 6.44. The published-config lead of DOC/MAC over NAC is budget-carried; mechanism-level ordering favors NAC at both tested budgets.

latency_grid_2026_10_13.description: Per-image counterattack latency (ms) for the unified grid: separates nominal step-size budget (alpha x K) from actual compute cost. Defense-only; attack generation excluded.
key_findings: NAC costs the same as TTC at both K (K2: 10.36 vs 10.58; K4: 18.99 vs 18.84) -- the look-ahead adds no measurable per-step cost.
At DOC's published budget (K=4 alpha=3/255) DOC costs 19.47ms while NAC at the same K=4 costs 18.99ms and scores +2.56pp higher (40.01 vs 37.45): NAC wins on both axes at matched budget.

MAC's published config costs 59.20ms (5.7x NAC K=2 at 10.36ms, 3.1x NAC K=4 at 18.99ms) for 44.89; at NAC's budget it costs 16.00ms (54% more than NAC) yet scores 6.44 vs NAC's 17.17. MAC is dominated by NAC at matched budget on both accuracy and latency.
pure_la costs ~1.8x TTC/NAC (extra look-ahead forward), so NAC's gain does NOT come from extra compute that pure lookahead would need.
